title: How to do due diligence on a person
summary: Who someone is, the companies they have run and how those ended, what the courts and the press have recorded, and what they left out.
body_markdown:
Start with the decision their background could change and the questions that follow from it. Confirm who the person is before you collect anything, so that records about a namesake stay out of the file, then test what they say about themselves against records they did not write: business registries, court records, news coverage and their public footprint over the years. Put anything material they did not mention to them directly, and write up each finding with its source and how confident you are.


They are different things. Business due diligence on a person uses public records, such as company registries, court records, news and the person's own public footprint, to research the people behind a counterparty, an investment or a partnership. A consumer background check is a separate service, and Sixtyfour does not run those.


Far enough to cover the career the decision rests on: often the last ten years for someone running a company, and every company named in their pitch. Registries set limits of their own. Companies House's free service holds every company dissolved since January 2010, and the Individual Insolvency Register in England and Wales usually removes a record within three months of the case ending, so older bankruptcies are looked for in The Gazette.


In the US, search the PACER Case Locator, a national index of the federal district, bankruptcy and appellate courts, and then the state courts where the person and their companies have lived and done business, since most cases are filed in state courts. In England and Wales, search the Individual Insolvency Register and The Gazette. Then open the docket and the filings, because a complaint is one side's allegations and most civil cases end before trial.


Run the same checks in the other direction. Confirm their identity, list the companies and funds they say they have run or backed and check each one in the registries and in any Form D filings that name them, search the courts and the news, and compare how they have described their career over the years. Then talk to people who worked with them, including founders whose companies did not succeed.


First confirm that the record is about them, and read the record itself. Then put it to the person and ask for their account, record their answer as their own statement, and check what you can of it. Decide whether it matters by asking whether it changes the decision, and write down what stays open.
